@keerthanpg @ArtirKel The original paperclip scenario doesn't specify *how* the AI learned the goal of maximizing paperclips.

In the report (updated a lot from the version you read) I argue that generalization to large-scale goals is likely for policies which use high-level concepts, like AGIs will.

I'm also excited about more widespread engagement with the alignment problem. Whether you agree or disagree with my claims in this thread, the stakes of the situation justify robust debate and in-depth analysis. Feedback and discussion very welcome; let's figure this problem out!

How can we prevent AGI misalignment? I'm most excited about work on scalable oversight (theory: https://t.co/LZqCPtcD0D; practice: https://t.co/i3HreKCpyf) and mechanistic interpretability (https://t.co/Jq68YXXAas). See this curriculum for more: https://t.co/FZklkurzz7

It's hard to predict what happens next. But once AGIs are working against us, I'm not optimistic. The historical record shows that whoever produces the best tech (by this point, AGIs themselves) comes to dominate the world. One way that might happen: https://t.co/D84xf9xJ47

Fundamentally these are claims about inductive biases, which wouldn't apply to a lookup-table "AGI". But realistic AGIs will do instrumental reasoning, which will bias them towards power-seeking generalization - like preventing us from shutting them down. https://t.co/moFhCP0Rcq

This is a form of goal misgeneralization: https://t.co/W0RX49xnUt. AGIs will understand that that “obey humans in a non-manipulative way” is one possible generalization of “obey humans”—but almost no other possible generalizations will rule out power-seeking manipulation.

We'll try to train AGIs to follow constraints like honesty, but that won't scale as they become superhuman. Analogously, an adult constrained to be honest can still persuade a child to approve of actions which are very harmful, like eating food which happens to be poisonous.

Turner et al. formalize the intuitive claim that power-seeking is often very useful. So while we can’t predict which misaligned goals AGIs will develop, AGIs will likely find power-seeking strategies which achieve those goals by disempowering humans. https://t.co/R0rWrPM1C5

But by Bostrom's instrumental convergence thesis (https://t.co/mxE81Eww7y), almost all large-scale goals lead to instrumental goals like survival, resource acquisition, etc - just because these are so robustly useful. As Russell puts it, you can’t fetch coffee if you’re dead!

Situationally-aware policies will be able to get higher reward by deliberately exploiting our mistakes - e.g. by lying about their goals, trying to earn our trust, etc. Advanced AIs will be very good at modelling humans (there's a lot of data!) so this will be hard to catch.

2. Some goals are instrumentally useful across many environments (curiosity, making money, etc) which will teach policies to value them. If they're correlated with reward often enough, policies may rarely see data which teaches them to prioritize alignment over these other goals.

The policy was trained with human feedback to grab a ball, but learned to hold the claw between camera and ball to fool evaluators. This example is trivial, but consistent errors might teach policies to try to *seem* helpful rather than *being* helpful. https://t.co/VAsEQ7F72t

But these examples are all task-specific; why might misaligned goals correlate with reward across many tasks, and generalize to new tasks? Consider two broad reasons:
1. Consistent flaws in our evaluation procedures. E.g. can you spot the problem in this gif? https://t.co/cE4qkjsPVj

The goals policies learn will depend on the reward functions we train them on. Krakovna et al. give many examples of misspecified rewards which lead to a range of misbehavior - RL learns to exploit even very subtle misspecifications! https://t.co/joS2JksW8j

I'm unsure if existing networks have goals in this sense. But Jaderberg et al find neurons that "code directly for important game states" in their deep RL policy. It seems very likely that AGIs will use high-level outcome-representations to choose actions. https://t.co/GTfOUDyFEh

In the report I outline an illustrative deep reinforcement learning training setup, then discuss three phases of training I expect to see:
1. Learning to plan towards achieving goals
2. Pursuing goals in a situationally-aware way
3. Generalizing goals beyond human supervision

Alignment arguments are often very abstract because we lack empirical data or solid theory for AGI. But that's exactly why the problem seems hard to solve, and why we should work to build those theories in advance! If we don't, we may have little time to catch up as we near AGI.

To start, why think about this now? ML progress has been astonishingly rapid over the last decade. And surveys show many top ML researchers expect AGI within decades. So if misalignment is plausible we should do our best to understand the core problem. https://t.co/EhJrNKEvpc

text:
To summarize my values, I care about:
- the welfare of all beings, present and future (intrinsic care-morality)
- the agency of all currently-existing beings (intrinsic cooperation-morality)
- being cooperative in order to achieve these (instrumental cooperation-morality) 7/8

Since it’s so hard to deduce the instrumental benefits of cooperation-morality, evolution made us care intrinsically about cooperative principles, which carries over even to cases where they're no longer useful. So cooperation is more than just an instrumental strategy. 6/8

Because
A) Like in economics, the benefits come via complex multi-agent dynamics
B) We reason using causal decision theories which don't account for others predicting our actions. Cooperation is more intuitively useful under functional decision theory: https://t.co/303VTASxPc 5/8

Many intuitions which seem strange from a care-morality view make more sense under cooperation-morality, like:
- The act-omission distinction
- Person-affecting population ethics
- Deontological rules 

Why is it hard to deduce the instrumental benefits of these intuitions? 4/8

When you’re in a multi-agent environment, though, others respond to your choices in complex ways which make cooperation-morality instrumentally useful. E.g. a rule of absolute honesty is instrumentally useful if others can predict when you’ll lie. https://t.co/Zk6DS5s0Rr 3/8

An extreme example of care-morality is hedonic utilitarianism, which only treats others as moral patients, not moral agents. Care-morality implicitly assumes your decisions are the only thing that matter. In one sense that’s true: your actions are all you can affect. 2/8

Many conflicts between ethical intuitions arise from failing to distinguish between morality as care vs morality as cooperation. Care-morality means looking after others’ welfare. Cooperation-morality means upholding their agency, e.g. by not deceiving or disempowering them. 1/8

@Utilit_Aria Also I think there's very commonly self-deception about how effective conformist strategies are, because being conformist is nice and safe. But if you look at how conformist major reformers were throughout history, it does seem like weird but principled stances get a long way!

text: You can think of difficulty in terms of searching for hypotheses. Even explaining in detail why X is wrong still leaves open any possibility apart from X. Saying "Y is underrated" specifies a broad direction. Saying "here's how Y works" requires constructing a whole new theory.

Important to remember that it's *much* easier to identify flaws in other people's ideas than to construct correct ideas yourself.

In particular, "people overrate X" is easier than "people underrate Y" is easier than "I know how Y works".

Overall, solving this puzzle isn't a priority for me, but I think of it as one datapoint to help ground big-picture abstractions about competition and cooperation (like how insect colonies provide a metaphor for thinking about society).

Blog post version: https://t.co/l8c51fNTHF

A counterargument: males in some species don’t compete via shows of force - e.g. birds which sing to attract mates. Maybe this is because 90% of birds are monogamous, though (vs <5% of mammals), which promotes labour specialisation. Do all non-monogamous males compete physically?

If true, it feels a bit sad: there could be a much better solution if it weren’t for the threat of physical force. But it does seem pretty plausible to me - especially because hermaphroditism is much more common in plants, which can’t use the strategy of physical dominance.

6. Physical dominance.

Maybe male competition is grounded in physical power, so dominant males could just prevent hermaphrodites (who invest less in muscle and brawn) from impregnating anyone. So sexes aren't a solution to an environmental problem, but to a coordination problem.

This effect plausibly occurs in plants (https://t.co/n60jrM3eiF) but not strongly enough to prevent most of them from being hermaphroditic. Maybe the plant-animal divergence is driven by a combination of this and the previous options. But I think the 6th option is the strongest:

5. Self-fertilisation

Perhaps self-fertilisation has a strong short-term advantage, despite losing out on the long-term benefits of sex (https://t.co/J47rIKwQg8). If hermaphrodites often evolve ways to self-fertilise, group selection could prevent hermaphroditism from spreading.

But on timeframes where sexual desires can themselves evolve, we should expect stabilising sexual selection towards the best combination of fertility and attractiveness. I.e. why doesn't everyone end up most attracted to whoever seems like the best hermaphrodite?

4. Difficulty of fixating hermaphroditism.

A hermaphrodite in a species without many hermaphrodites is likely not as attractive to females as most males are, nor as fertile as most females are. So maybe even after arising in a few individuals, the trait will be selected against.

3. Difficulty of evolving hermaphroditism.

But non-reproductive hermaphroditism arises via mutations pretty frequently, so I’d be surprised if reproductive hermaphroditism were unachievable. And there are a few hermaphroditic animals - so why haven’t they spread more widely?

2. Developmental or metabolic costs of being hermaphroditic.

Maybe having two sets of functional sex organs is just a very expensive adaptation? But this seems unlikely to be the main factor - the relevant baseline is the existence of males at all, which is a huge energy cost.

1. Specialisation of labour

If there’s a strong division of labour between males and females, maybe it’s harder for hermaphrodites to gather enough resources to support offspring. But in many species males contribute little - eg orang-utans, who are very solitary.

And in fact, most plants are hermaphroditic - so why aren’t animals, apart from a handful? A quick search doesn’t turn up any widely accepted answer, so I’ve brainstormed a few possibilities. I’m not a biologist and may well be missing something big; if so, please let me know.

It's pretty clear why sex itself happens - gene exchange is very valuable (e.g. see https://t.co/9Owql5mUUh). But a species with only hermaphrodites could get all the genetic benefits of sex, without the massive cost of half its population being unable to bear offspring.

One thing I really like about evolutionary biology is that many seemingly-basic questions are still areas of active research.

Here’s one I’ve been thinking about, which I haven’t seen a satisfactory answer to: evolutionarily speaking, why aren’t we all hermaphrodites?

Perhaps it’s worth considering what differences you’d expect in a world where this is true vs false. (For example, might you expect that the highest-status men actually don’t spend much time dancing, drinking, or even socialising?) 16/N

If I were more cynical I'd say that the “fun” part of high-status fun is also a strategic ambiguity to facilitate status transactions - if people couldn’t convince themselves and others that they were having fun, their attempts to seem prestigious would be much more obvious. 15/N

Basically the same dynamics play out internationally as well - promoters offer girls free flights, food and accommodation in exchange for attendance at nightclubs in St Tropez, etc. On those trips the transactionality is usually a bit more obvious. 14/N

In some sense the whole system is grounded in the models’ sex appeal, but I think the models’ prestige is just as important - models are preferred to women who most men find more attractive, as well as preferred to women who have more transactional attitudes towards sex. 13/N

Promoters are disproportionately black; Mears talks about them having “colour capital”, and using some stereotypes to their advantage in order to catch attention. They need to be very charismatic and attractive to convince girls to come along without seeming transactional. 12/N

The nightclub profits by creating an atmosphere of “suspended reality” where a large group of people who all individually believe that buying status in this way is tacky can still convince themselves that all the other people don’t think it’s tacky. 11/N

The markup on champagne is determined not by the amount of champagne, but by how ostentatious the purchase is. The biggest purchases, costing >100k per bottle, come with elaborate fanfare: all music stops, spotlights shine on the buyer, a train of staff bring it out, etc. 10/N

Everyone selects for models even when they don’t personally find the model look attractive, because the fashion industry established it as the Schelling look for high-status women. (For more, see Mears’ other book, Pricing Beauty; and my tweet below.) 9/N

Some other interesting observations: 7/N

And most are careful not to ruin their reputations by accepting cash from promoters. Instead, to bring enough girls, promoters each need to do a bunch of emotional labour, flirting, relationship-building, and many non-cash payments (food, transport, even accommodation). 6/N

The nightclubs pay “promoters” to scout out and bring along dozens of beautiful women each night. Those women get access to an exclusive venue with many wealthy men - but by itself that’s not enough to motivate regular attendance, at least not from the prettiest. 5/N

Instead an ecosystem develops to sell sufficient strategic ambiguity to allow (self- and other-) deception about the transaction taking place, by incorporating a series of middlemen.

To start, men pay thousands for table charges and already-expensive drinks at 5-20x markups. 4/N

But explicit transactions between different forms of cultural capital are low-status - it demonstrates that you can’t get the other forms directly. So the wealthy men can’t just pay the beautiful women to come party with them. 3/N

Some activities which are often fun - dancing, drinking, socialising - become much more fun when you're also feeling high-status. So wealthy men want to buy the feeling of high-status fun, by partying alongside other high-status people, particularly beautiful women. 2/N

New York’s nightclubs are the particle accelerators of sociology: reliably creating precise conditions under which exotic extremes of status-seeking behaviour can be observed.

On the other hand, this means most students won't be far from the median. So the marginal additional acceptance will seem pretty similar to existing students, but plausibly drag down the mean much more than expected if you weren't accounting for long tails.

This shouldn't be surprising, because it's how scientists often discover new phenomena. But it's easy to assume that the interface adds so much it can't be sidestepped.

Same for business - big corps are the standard interface for doing stuff, but entrepreneurs see past that.

Concrete example: science is an interface for learning about the world. It's one of the most successful interfaces ever, featuring many valuable tools, norms and methods. Yet in many domains you can still move beyond scientific knowledge by playing around with what interests you.

There's a systematic reason for this: creating interfaces that map onto the structure of reality is really hard, and preserving them under competitive pressure even harder. So there are cracks in everything. But few people are looking for them, because that's effortful and weird.

Modern society often feels like many layers of interfaces between individuals and reality. But reality is usually much more accessible than you expect - if you bypass the interfaces you can just reach out, touch it, and make things happen.

Whereas TikTok produces entertainment, while sucking in a *lot* of kids' time. What's the counterfactual? Perhaps participating in more local social status games, where the payoffs are more equal. Or in career games (the value of which depends very much on how you play them).

If a social media platform gave scientists a lot of status based on posts about their scientific achievements, that'd be great. It wouldn't reward work on the platform much, but it'd reward much more valuable work off it. (Google Scholar kinda does this, and LinkedIn a bit too.)

Now, usually regarding the creation of value is better than rewarding the showcasing of value, because it rewards productivity and helps disrupt existing hierarchies. But it depends a lot on the type of value in each case, and what effort put into pursuing that value displaces.

TikTok and YouTube are far on the proof of work end: everyone needs to put in a huge amount of work, and so the advantage from having existing status is much lower.

That's why they've created many more internet celebrities than any of the other platforms I mentioned.

Proof of work creates value. Proof of stake showcases value. LinkedIn is the purest proof of stake platform; nobody's there for the content.

Instagram and Twitter are in the middle - you put work into posts, but they often rely on existing traits (beauty, interestingness, etc).

There's a fantastic essay by @eugenewei about how social media platforms provide "status as a service" via "proof of work". If you haven't read it yet, you definitely should: https://t.co/PtI420mE3p

Riffing off that: I think we can extend the analogy to cover proof of stake too.

I also agree with Eliezer that most attempted solutions miss the point. And I'm sympathetic to his quote below. But I'd say the same is true of his style of reasoning: when your big seemingly-flawless abstraction implies 99% chance of doom, you're right less than half the time. https://t.co/MMkYGsMAuX

Note that, although I'm taking the "easy" side, I agree with Eliezer that AI misalignment is a huge risk which is dramatically understudied, and should be a key priority of those who want to make the future of humanity go well.

My key argument here: humans were optimised very hard by evolution for achieving goals, and much less hard for intellectual research. So if we optimise AIs for the latter, then when they first surpass us at that, it seems unlikely that they'll be as agentic as we are now.

3. Now, as AIs get more intelligent I agree that they'll eventually become arbitrarily agentic. But the key question (which Scott unfortunately omits) is: will early superhuman intelligences be worryingly agentic? If they're not, we can use them to do superhuman safety research.

In this frame, making a tool AI into a consequentialist agent is therefore less like "connect model to output device" and more like "give model many new skills involving motivation, attention, coherence, metacognition, etc". Which seems much less likely to happen by accident.

Thinking in terms of "motivational systems" makes agency less binary. We all know humans who are very smart and very lazy. And the space of AI minds is much broader, so we should expect that it contains very smart AIs that are much less goal-directed than low-motivation humans.

2. Scott describes non-agentic AI as one which "doesn’t realize the universe exists, or something to that effect? It just likes connecting premises to conclusions." A framing I prefer: an AI that's very good at pattern-matching but lacks a well-developed motivational system.

1. Scott describes my position as similar to Eric Drexler's CAIS framework. But Drexler's main focus is modularity, which he claims leads to composite systems that aren't dangerously agentic. Whereas I instead expect unified non-modular AGIs; for more, see https://t.co/ZqroJLpwIN

text: I do think most people should aim to make their best friendships significantly more committed. Maybe this is inconsistent. But ideally what you get out of a close, committed friendship is quite different from what you get out of a 2nd relationship (e.g. no messy sexual dynamics).

The original argument also weighs against committing hard to friends and family. But very few people commit to friends anywhere near as strongly as partners (e.g. living with them indefinitely). And strong commitments to parents do strain relationships (esp. in asian families).

A few other points that come to mind: I think people in my circles are unusually good at the type of communication which makes relationships thrive. But they're also unusually individualistic and career-focused, so maybe this cancels out overall?

Overall I still feel pretty uncertain what relationship style is best for people similar to me. By nature I'm the sort of person for whom aiming at the best possible outcome feels very compelling, and most risks don't. But it'll likely depend on my eventual (primary) partner.

And a counterresponse: sure, but that's high-variance! If very deep commitment is so crucial, why tempt fate through actions which invoke many of our strongest and most unreasonable instincts?

OTOH if there's any experience which makes that risk worthwhile, it's falling in love.

To me the most compelling response is that, done well, poly strengthens commitment, by making you work through a series of tricky trust exercises. (This response is more applicable to hierarchical than non-hierarchical poly relationships, but the former seem much more common.)

Imo the best argument against polyamory, which I've seldom heard, is not about love or sex, but rather commitment. You can't have two top priorities, and I'd guess returns to more commitment and psychological safety remain very high well past the point most relationships reach.

Why is it so hard to imagine utopias? Because progress is less about extrapolating trend lines and more about inventing new trends. Figuring out which types of change could lead to a radically better world is half the work.

Note that these aren't necessarily criticisms of the concepts as used by experts in the relevant fields - in several cases I just started off with a naively optimistic impression of them.

Also, since it's a long list, I'm probably wrong about at least one of these. But which?

Pleasure/suffering: see Buddhism

Personal identity: same, plus Parfit

Most ML theory: doesn't help scale deep learning

Planning: when did you last make a plan with 3+ steps? Abstraction does most of the work

Rationality: mostly just nudges intelligence in the right direction

Fitness: is only defined locally, with respect to a population

GDP: same, GDP comparisons over time are very hacky

Welfare: you can't untangle selfish vs altruistic preferences

International law: see IR realism

The scientific method: *what* scientific method? See Strevens

Ten abstractions that turned out to be much less robust than I'd expected:
- Evolutionary fitness
- GDP
- Economic welfare
- International law
- The scientific method
- Pleasure/suffering
- Personal identity
- Most ML theory
- Planning
- Rationality

But "it's just syntactics" isn't right either.

So I'm trying "it's just definitions" as my critique of pointless debates.

In other words: thinking of statements or hypotheses as the fundamental units of reasoning is misleading. Instead, think of reasoning as the manipulation of mental models. You wouldn't call a model true or false, or assign a probability to it, except in unusually clear-cut cases.

text: @fordacious Because of incompleteness there will always be edge cases, but no human concepts are meant to be fully formal anyway. My prediction is that this definition works pretty well for the type of universe we find ourselves in.

What do I mean by pattern? In general, a structure which can be recognised by some computable algorithm. For our purposes: a structure which can be recognised/understood by the human algorithm (or similar algorithms, e.g. AGIs which understand our universe).

To be more specific: concepts are patterns which arise in minds, and minds are a type of computable algorithm, and computable algorithms are equivalent to Turing Machines, and Turing Machines are a mathematical construction. (And maths in turn is grounded in logic, e.g. via ZFC.)

We inhabit a physical universe of objects and forces and an abstract universe of ideas and thoughts. Physics showed that the former consists of high-level patterns of quarks, etc. Turing showed that the latter consists of high-level patterns in math: an equally crucial reduction.

4 premises:
1. We’ll build AIs which are much more intelligent than humans.
2. Those AIs will be autonomous agents which pursue large-scale goals.
3. Those goals will be misaligned with ours.
4. The development of such AIs would lead to them gaining control of humanity’s future.

The core claim: human intelligence allows us to build complex societies and advanced technology to control the world. But AIs will eventually become more capable than us at these types of tasks. If they don’t want to obey us, then humanity might lose control over its future.

Given how bold these claims are, I think it's important that people who take them seriously try hard to explicate them clearly. And there's a lot of room to do so, as I emphasise in the report. It's 15k words but could have been 150k given more time.

Or consider the continuum between a physicist talking about special relativity, vs a layperson who can't distinguish it from general relativity, vs someone who can't distinguish it from Newton's laws, vs a child saying those words without knowing what a scientific theory is.

By accepting continuity of reference, you can make rigid designators less rigid. "A version of Aristotle who died young" refers. "A version of Aristotle born in the year 2000" refers much less. "A version of Aristotle born in 2000 with the same genes as me" barely refers at all.

One must always crop and contort the world to squeeze it into a human-comprehemsible conceptual framework. The question is always merely: how much is lost in the process? Or (to use a CS term that really should become more common): how leaky are our abstractions?

I'm now thinking that the most important thing to make continuous is reference itself. When I mention a name or description, I'm using a concept formulated at a high level of abstraction. So there's always vagueness when mapping it to the real world.

Lastly, decentralisation makes it unusually misleading to judge movements by headline examples, because it's so hard to tell who endorses them. To think clearly on these issues, we must internalise that social media polarises not just the outgroup, but you and I.

This all means we should be very careful in pattern-matching current social movements to historical examples (for good or ill). Their decentralisation makes them stronger but less coherent; it makes examples of their misbehavior more salient and more common but less important.

Does this leave a power vacuum? Yes, but it's not easily fillable. Within feminism the influence of aggressive men is constrained. Meanwhile the public faces of climate and animal advocacy are children and celebrities: it's hard to build a power bloc of future people and animals.

Meanwhile the fringes push radical ideas without anyone to rein them in. But they also lack any central authority as backup. The Twitter firehose provides reinforcements, but that's fickle and short-lived. So there's less long-term pressure, and very little organised violence.

You also get more idealistic movements, since the loudest voices don't have to struggle to implement policies in messy reality. Indeed, there are no consistently loudest voices - rather, what's broadcast is a tapestry of thousands of "15 minutes of fame".

Of course these movements draw on existing scholarship, but they are less able to translate it from specialist terminology to authoritative public-facing manifestos. This also limits the extent to which opponents can push back by directly critiquing the core concepts.

In exchange, they have much less legibility and message discipline. It's far less clear what they stand for, their core tenets, or what their terminology even means. Lately you see this with "defund the police" crowdsourcing definitions in realtime. https://t.co/z0OQ3SysUE
